text: Today I want to talk about the infamous gender pay gap. Is it true that women earn 82 cents for every dollar a man earns? Or is it a lie constructed by media and propagated by feminists? Let's figure it out. First, let's talk about where the idea of the gender pay gap actually comes from. You can say its modern roots go back to the early 20th century when women entered the workforce in large numbers, especially during wars, and it soon became clear that they were often paid less than men for similar jobs. This led to political slogans like equal pay for equal work, which eventually resulted in the Equal Pay Act of 1963 in the U.S., making it illegal to pay men and women differently for the same job. Passing that law was a huge step, but it still seemed that women were earning less than men overall, which led to more questions. Economists started asking, even if discrimination is illegal, why do women still earn less overall? In the 1970s, economists like Jacob Mencer and Solomon Polacek developed models explaining wage differences using factors like education, experience, and time out of the workforce. This introduced the idea that part of the gap can be explained by these factors, while part of it remains unexplained. So far, everything seems quite logical. But what happened next is interesting. As the topic moved from academia research into public discussion, the nuance started to get simplified. Media and activism, including feministic movement, tend to favor clear, simple messages, because those get attention. And this is where the infamous 82 cents on the dollar comes in. By the way, this number, which is commonly associated with data from U.S. Census Bureau and Bureau of Labor Statistics, represents median earnings of all working men compared to median earnings of all working women. Not averages, like some people believe. But what is the problem with this number? Well, here is the key point. This number does not adjust for factors like profession, hours worked, experience, career breaks, and so on. It is simply a broad comparison across all workers. So when you actually try to compare apples to apples, same occupation, same experience, same working hours, and so on, the gap drops quite a lot. Instead of 15 to 20%, it usually ends up in the low single digits, somewhere around 2 to 6%. And this is not just one paper. You see this pattern across OECD, EU, and U.S. research. But what about this 2 to 6%? Do these numbers represent discrimination against women? Well, it is difficult to say for sure. You see, even across large data sets, it is hard to control for every single factor. It could be discrimination. But it could also reflect things like negotiation, career choices, willingness to take risks or stressful roles, ambition, or other variables that are hard to measure. So what do we have overall? Even though women earning 82 cents on the dollar is factually not wrong, it is at the very least misleading, as it does not account for important factors. And once we try to have apples to apples comparison, accounting for profession, experience, hours worked, and so on, the gap drops significantly, on average to around 2 to 6%. And that remaining part is simply the portion we cannot fully explain with the data we have.
